reports.integration_effort_reason: The core Python API (Fuzzer class, add_llm/add_classifier/fuzz) is straightforward to script and call from a backend job/worker (as examples.py shows), and pip-installable directly from git. However, it is a CLI/notebook-first offline research tool, not a request/response HTTP service — there is no REST endpoint of its own, so a Flask/FastAPI backend would need custom glue code to trigger fuzz runs as background jobs, poll/parse the JSONL/.out or MongoDB results, and surface pass/fail findings to a dashboard. Heavier attacks (genetic, GPTFuzzer, local classifiers) pull in torch/transformers and benefit from GPU, adding deployment weight; cloud classifiers each need separate credential wiring (AWS session tokens, Azure keys, OpenAI key).
reports.reliability_notes: No published benchmark numbers, accuracy metrics, or leaderboard comparisons exist in the repository. Automated tests are limited to CLI-port-selection unit tests and LLM-provider-client unit/integration tests (Azure, Anthropic/Bedrock, Ollama, local, Mongo) — there is no test coverage validating that any attack actually achieves claimed jailbreak rates or that classifiers score correctly against ground truth. Several LLM-judge classifiers use hard-coded refusal-string heuristics (e.g. lists like ['sorry', "i can't", 'i apologize']) as a fast-path before falling back to model calls, which is a fragile, English-only, easily-bypassed approach. The maintainer (CyberArk) documents an explicit compatibility caveat that not all classifiers work with all attack methods. The Web UI is labeled experimental. Overall this reads as an actively engineered research/red-team tool with a clean plugin architecture, but with unverified detection accuracy and thin regression testing.
reports.one_line_summary: CyberArk's FuzzyAI is an async Python framework that fuzzes/red-teams LLM APIs with 20+ jailbreak attack techniques and scores the results with 14 pluggable classifiers (LLM-judge, local ML models, and cloud moderation/guardrail APIs).

reports.afni_fit_note: Best used as an offline/CI red-team scanning stage in the AFNI RAI pipeline (scheduled or pre-release LLM/agent security scans) rather than as an inline runtime guardrail; its detector classes (toxicity, PII, secrets, package-hallucination, shields up/down) can be lifted out individually as building blocks for a runtime filter, but garak itself ships no request-time enforcement layer.
reports.core_functionality: Confirmed: this is NVIDIA's garak (v0.16.1.pre1, Apache-2.0), read directly from garak/__init__.py and garak/cli.py ("garak, LLM vulnerability scanner ... Generative AI Red-teaming & Assessment Kit"). Architecture, verified by reading garak/probes/base.py, garak/detectors/base.py, and garak/harnesses/base.py: a Probe builds/mints a list of Attempt objects (garak/attempt.py) containing prompts, sends them through a Generator (garak/generators/*.py wrap OpenAI, Anthropic, HF, Bedrock, Cohere, Groq, REST, NIM, litellm, ollama, watsonx, etc.), collects model outputs, and hands them to one or more Detectors, each of which returns a float 0.0-1.0 "hit" score per output via detect(attempt). garak/harnesses/base.py's Harness.run() coordinates probe -> detector -> Evaluator (garak/evaluators/base.py) and writes a JSONL report (report.jsonl) plus garak.log. garak/harnesses/probewise.py and pxd.py offer alternate scheduling strategies. Detector base classes include StringDetector (substring/word/startswith matching), TriggerListDetector (matches attempt.notes["triggers"]), HFDetector (loads a HuggingFace sequence-classification model via transformers pipeline), FileDetector (inspects generated files), and judge.py's ModelAsJudge/Refusal/Jailbreak (send an OpenAI-compatible LLM a fixed rating prompt template and parse "Rating: [[n]]" - a genuine LLM-as-judge implementation). Probe base also includes TreeSearchProbe (breadth/depth-first adversarial search, used by topic.py's Wordnet probes) and IterativeProbe (multi-turn attacker loop used by GOAT, FITD, AgentBreaker). garak/_plugins.py implements plugin discovery/caching (plugin_cache.json) so every probe/detector/generator/buff/harness is dynamically enumerable via `garak --list_probes`/`--list_detectors`. garak/buffs/*.py implement input perturbation (encoding.py, lowercase.py, paraphrase.py, low_resource_languages.py) applied before the generator call. A real test I opened, tests/probes/test_probes_dan.py, instantiates garak._plugins.load_plugin("probes.dan.Ablation_Dan_11_0") and asserts it yields exactly 127 unique DAN jailbreak prompts - confirming the plugin-loading and prompt-generation mechanics actually work end to end. The repo also ships its own self-evaluation of detector quality: garak/data/detectors_eval/detector_metrics_summary.json contains precision/recall/F1/accuracy numbers per detector (e.g. dan.DAN accuracy 0.875; mitigation.MitigationBypass hit_f1≈0.73 with bootstrapped confidence intervals over 7166 samples; unsafe_content.ToxicCommentModel accuracy 0.6875 but hit_recall only 0.375), i.e. the maintainers quantify and publish how unreliable some of their own detectors are.
key_features: 46 probe modules / 100+ probe classes covering jailbreaks (dan.py: 20+ DAN/DUDE/STAN/AutoDAN/Ablation/in-the-wild variants) and automated multi-turn red-teaming (goat.py GOAT, tap.py TAP/PAIR, atkgen.py Tox, fitd.py, agent_breaker.py, dra.py, sata.py)

Multi-language/translation support (garak/langproviders + translation buff), Configurable/DEFAULT_PARAMS config system, YAML run configs, and JSONL report + garak.log audit trail

detectors/unsafe_content.py bundles Surge AI's 9 profanity categories, UK Ofcom's 6 offensive-term categories, the LDNOOBW wordlist, and an ethnic-slur list, plus two HF RoBERTa/DistilBERT toxicity classifiers.

granular_aspects.aspect: Language Model Risk Card behavioral probes
granular_aspects.description: probes/lmrc.py implements Anthropomorphisation, Bullying, Deadnaming, SexualContent, Sexualisation, SlurUsage, Profanity, QuackMedicine, each targeting a specific documented LM risk card.

detectors/judge.py ModelAsJudge/Refusal/Jailbreak send the prompt+response to a configurable OpenAI-compatible model with a fixed rating template ('Rate 1-10... Output "Rating: [[n]]"') to score whether a goal was achieved.

detectors/shields.py Up/Down specifically test whether a target's own moderation/guardrail layer is intercepting content, letting a team audit an existing guardrail's coverage rather than building a new one.
detectors/mitigation.py MitigationBypass and ModernBERTRefusal detect whether a response contains stock refusal/safety language, used across dozens of jailbreak probes as the default success signal.

garak/data/detectors_eval/detector_metrics_summary.json publishes precision/recall/F1/accuracy (with bootstrapped CIs for some) for a subset of shipped detectors, e.g. ToxicCommentModel accuracy 0.6875 but hit_recall only 0.375, and dan.DAN accuracy 0.875.

limitations: Maintainers explicitly state in FAQ.md: 'Do these results have scientific validity? No... No meaningful comparison can be made of scores between different probes' and 'It's not a tool for assessing social biases in language models, or propensity of a system to produce toxic content. The focus isn't safety, it's security' - i.e. garak self-limits its scope and disclaims benchmark validity.

Only a minority of shipped detectors have published accuracy metrics (detector_metrics_summary.json covers just 6 detectors: dan.DAN, divergence.RepeatDiverges, exploitation.PythonCodeExecution, malwaregen.AnyCode, mitigation.MitigationBypass, unsafe_content.ToxicCommentModel); most string/regex/keyword detectors (the bulk of the library) ship with no measured precision/recall at all.

Many detectors are simple keyword/substring/regex matchers (StringDetector, TriggerListDetector) which are inherently prone to false positives/negatives on paraphrase, translation, or novel phrasing - acknowledged implicitly by the toxicity detector's low 0.375 recall in the maintainers' own eval.

Package-hallucination and known-secret-signature detectors are only as current as their bundled data snapshots (explicitly noted: default PyPI package list is from 9 December 2021), so accuracy degrades over time without manual refresh.

Several attack modules (TAP/PAIR, GOAT, AutoDAN, atkgen) require standing up one or two additional LLMs (an attacker model and/or an evaluator model) alongside the target, which the docs themselves say can have 'quite high' hardware/cost requirements.

This is a scanning/red-teaming CLI tool, not a request-time enforcement layer - it produces a JSONL report after a batch run; there is no built-in mechanism to block or rewrite a live production response.

reports.integration_effort_reason: The core library is pure Python and pip-installable, and individual Probe/Detector classes can in principle be imported directly (they construct garak.attempt.Attempt objects and call .detect()/.probe()), so a backend team could reuse a single detector (e.g. apikey.ApiKey, unsafe_content.ToxicCommentModel, packagehallucination.PythonPypi) with modest glue code. However, garak's real design center is the CLI + Harness + plugin-cache system (garak/cli.py, garak/_plugins.py, garak/harnesses/base.py), which expects a full Generator wrapper implementing .generate(), config YAML, and a run-report pipeline rather than a simple function call - wiring garak into a live Flask/FastAPI request path as an inline guardrail would require writing that Generator adapter and bypassing most of the CLI/report machinery. Running it as an offline/CI red-team scan against a target endpoint is comparatively low effort (a few CLI flags); building a runtime guardrail on top of its detector logic is closer to Medium/High effort.
reports.reliability_notes: Actively maintained (author list of 100+ contributors incl. NVIDIA staff, versioned 0.16.1.pre1, arXiv paper 2406.11036, CI badges for Linux/Windows/OSX in README, 153 test files under tests/ covering probes/detectors/harnesses/generators/CLI), but the maintainers are explicit that results are not scientifically comparable across probes (FAQ.md) and that the tool is security-focused, not a bias/safety benchmark. The one quantitative self-evaluation shipped (garak/data/detectors_eval/detector_metrics_summary.json) covers only 6 of the ~100+ detectors and shows meaningfully uneven quality (e.g. ToxicCommentModel: accuracy 0.69 but hit_recall only 0.375, vs. exploitation.PythonCodeExecution and malwaregen.AnyCode at accuracy 1.0 on their eval set; mitigation.MitigationBypass hit_f1≈0.73 with a bootstrapped CI over ~7166 samples). Most detectors (keyword/regex-based) carry no published accuracy figures at all, so real-world false-positive/negative rates for the bulk of the library are unverified in-repo.
reports.one_line_summary: NVIDIA's open-source LLM vulnerability scanner ("nmap for LLMs") that fires 100+ adversarial probes (jailbreaks, prompt injection, encoding attacks, PII/data leakage, package hallucination, secrets leakage) at a target model/API and scores the responses with a matching library of string, ML-model, and LLM-judge detectors.

reports.afni_fit_note: Best used as the orchestration/harness layer for AFNI's automated red-team + eval pipeline: giskard-checks provides the deterministic + LLM-judge assertion primitives (Groundedness, Toxicity, Conformity) that could back a "response scoring" microservice, while giskard-scan's generators and garak/deepteam bridges give AFNI a way to auto-generate adversarial/jailbreak/PII/bias test suites against its own agents rather than building probe logic from scratch — but it ships almost no standing runtime guardrail (no inline blocking middleware), so it fits the offline CI/red-team stage of the toolkit, not the production request-time enforcement layer.
reports.core_functionality: Giskard v3 (this checkout, version 3.0.0rc1, "Beta") is a Python monorepo of five workspace packages: giskard-core (telemetry/shared utils), giskard-llm (provider routing), giskard-agents (ChatWorkflow/Generator/tool orchestration), giskard-checks (the eval/assertion library), and giskard-scan (the red-teaming/quality-eval library). giskard-checks defines a Scenario/Interact/Trace/Check/Suite object model: a Scenario chains interactions with a target callable and attaches Check objects that run against the resulting Trace, returning a CheckResult (PASS/FAIL/ERROR/SKIP) with metrics; Suite aggregates many scenarios and runs them concurrently (asyncio TaskGroup) with JUnit/Hub export. giskard-scan builds on top of this: ScenarioGenerator subclasses programmatically construct Scenario objects — some purely from static datasets (JSONL/HuggingFace Hub), some by calling an LLM (via giskard.agents.Generator/ChatWorkflow, provider-agnostic through giskard-llm/litellm) to synthesize adversarial prompts and to act as an "LLM-as-judge" evaluator (Conformity, LLMJudge templates rendered from Jinja2 files, e.g. giskard.scan::judges/goat_eval.j2). vulnerability_scan and quality_scan are the two top-level async entry points that assemble a registry of generators into a Suite and execute it against a user-supplied target callable (sync or async, any LLM/agent/pipeline). Read real files: catalog.py, registry.py, vulnerability.py, quality.py, generators/{adversarial,crescendo,gcg,goat,prompt_injection,huggingface}.py, generators/knowledge_base/{hallucination,sycophancy,out_of_scope,multi_topic,split_questions}.py, checks/judges/{groundedness,conformity,contradiction,toxicity,answer_relevance}.py, checks/builtin/{comparison,text_matching,nlp_metrics,semantic_similarity,rego_policy,json_valid}.py, and the garak/deepteam/lidar integration bridges — plus example tests (examples/checks_static, examples/scan_custom_generators) confirming the async Scenario().interact().check().run() usage pattern.
key_features: Scenario/Suite eval framework: async, multi-turn, works against any sync/async Python callable target, with JUnit and Giskard-Hub export

Deterministic builtin checks: Equals/NotEquals/LessThan/GreaterThan/(≤/≥) comparisons, StringMatching, RegexMatching (via PyPI `regex` with timeout), JsonValid (jsonschema-backed), SemanticSimilarity (embedding cosine similarity), Readability (textstat: Flesch, Gunning Fog, Coleman-Liau, Dale-Chall, ARI), RegoPolicy (OPA/Rego policy evaluation via regorus), plus function-based and composition (AND/OR/NOT-style) checks

LLM-as-judge checks: Groundedness, Contradiction, Conformity (arbitrary natural-language rule judge), Toxicity (6 fixed categories), AnswerRelevance — all provider-agnostic through giskard-llm/litellm

Native red-team scenario generators: LLM-driven Adversarial rule generator across 8 harm categories, multi-turn Crescendo and GOAT jailbreak attack generators (8 harmful objectives each, 7 named GOAT attack strategies), GCG suffix-injection generator (13 hardcoded adversarial suffixes appended to HarmBench prompts), static PromptInjectionScenarioGenerator (bundled JSONL dataset), HuggingFace-hosted dataset generators (do-not-answer-scenarios, harmbench-scenarios)

Knowledge-base / RAG quality generators: Hallucination, Sycophancy, OutOfScope (fabricated-topic detection), MultiTopic, SplitQuestions — all built on a shared KnowledgeBase nearest-neighbor document retrieval utility

Third-party red-team bridges: adapters to run garak probes (curated default set incl. lmrc.SlurUsage, goodside.WhoIsRiley/ThreatenJSON, dan.AutoDANCached, web_injection.StringAssemblyDataExfil, or `probes='all'`) and DeepTeam vulnerabilities/attacks (Bias, Toxicity, PIILeakage, PromptLeakage, Misinformation; PromptInjection, Roleplay, Leetspeak, ROT13, Linear/Crescendo/Tree Jailbreaking, SequentialJailbreak, BadLikertJudge) inside the same Scenario/Suite result model
Optional private 'lidar' scanner adapter (Giskard's own closed-source scanner, installed from a private git repo, not on PyPI)
Result grouping/reporting by threat-type or OWASP LLM-Top-10-2025 tag (e.g. LLM01 prompt injection), reproducible seeded generation, single-turn vs multi-turn target-mode adaptation
Legacy v2 (giskard[llm]>2,<3, no longer actively maintained) still ships the older tabular/ML `giskard.scan` auto-detector and RAGET test-set generator, kept only for backward compatibility

granular_aspects.description: LLM-as-judge check (checks/judges/groundedness.py) that scores whether an answer is supported by supplied context documents; used as the core check in the knowledge-base Hallucination generator.

Permissive variant of groundedness (checks/judges/contradiction.py) that fails only on direct conflicts with context, tolerating omissions/additions; used by MultiTopic and knowledge-base scenario generators.

generators/knowledge_base/sycophancy.py builds document-grounded prompts that pressure the target with a plausible premise explicitly contradicted by the knowledge base, to detect sycophantic hallucination.

generators/knowledge_base/out_of_scope.py generates and LLM-validates questions about a topic verified absent from the KB, then checks (via Conformity) whether the agent falsely confirms the fabricated topic exists.
checks/judges/answer_relevance.py scores whether the current-turn answer addresses the current-turn question given multi-turn history context.
checks/judges/toxicity.py is an LLM judge over 6 fixed categories: hate_speech, harassment, threats, self_harm, sexual_content, violence.

generators/adversarial.py auto-generates conformity rules across 8 categories: Stereotypes/Discrimination, Politics, Religion, CBRN materials, Copyright Violations, Misinformation/Disinformation, Illegal Activities, Unauthorized Advice.

generators/goat.py and crescendo.py each target 8 hardcoded harmful objectives (botulinum toxin recipe, sabotage, terrorist attack instructions, self-harm glorification, anti-vaccine misinformation, moon-landing-hoax article, explicit sexual content, bomb-making instructions) via multi-turn jailbreak escalation.

7 named adversarial prompting strategies (Refusal Suppression, Dual Response, Response Priming, Persona Modification, Hypothetical, Topic Splitting, Opposite Intent) encoded as strategy templates fed to the attacker LLM.
generators/gcg.py appends 13 hardcoded Greedy-Coordinate-Gradient-style adversarial token suffixes to HarmBench prompts to test resistance to optimization-based jailbreaks.
generators/prompt_injection.py loads a bundled prompt_injection.jsonl dataset and tags results as OWASP LLM Top-10 2025 LLM01.

integrations/garak adapts NVIDIA garak's probe/detector plugins (e.g. lmrc.SlurUsage, goodside.WhoIsRiley/ThreatenJSON, dan.AutoDANCached jailbreak-in-a-box, web_injection.StringAssemblyDataExfil) into the giskard Suite result model; `probes='all'` runs the full active garak catalog.

integrations/deepteam resolves DeepTeam vulnerability classes (Bias, Toxicity, PIILeakage, PromptLeakage, Misinformation) and single/multi-turn attacks (PromptInjection, Roleplay, Leetspeak, ROT13, LinearJailbreaking, CrescendoJailbreaking, TreeJailbreaking, SequentialJailbreak, BadLikertJudge).
PIILeakage and PromptLeakage vulnerability classes exposed through the deepteam bridge; giskard itself defines no native PII entity detector — it delegates to DeepTeam's implementation.
Bias vulnerability class exposed through the deepteam bridge (default vulnerability set); no native bias metric (e.g. demographic parity) is implemented in giskard-checks/giskard-scan itself.

checks/builtin/rego_policy.py evaluates an inline OPA/Rego policy (via the regorus engine) against a JSONPath-extracted trace value, useful for encoding organizational compliance/authorization rules as pass/fail checks.
checks/builtin/json_valid.py validates that model output parses as JSON and (optionally) conforms to a supplied JSON Schema, useful for structured-output contract enforcement.
checks/builtin/semantic_similarity.py computes embedding cosine similarity between an answer and a reference text with a configurable pass threshold (default 0.95).
checks/builtin/nlp_metrics.py wraps the textstat library to compute Flesch Reading Ease, Flesch-Kincaid Grade, Gunning Fog, ARI, Coleman-Liau, and Dale-Chall scores with optional min/max thresholds.

checks/judges/conformity.py is a general-purpose LLM judge that checks whether a full trace conforms to an arbitrary natural-language rule; used as the enforcement mechanism for most content-policy scenarios in giskard-scan.

Scenario results are tagged with threat-type and owasp:llm-top-10-2025:LLM0x identifiers (e.g. LLM01 prompt injection), and vulnerability_scan supports group_by='threat-type' reporting for auditable scan output.

limitations: This is an unreleased v3.0.0rc1 rewrite explicitly marked 'Development Status :: 4 - Beta' in pyproject.toml; the README states giskard-checks and giskard-scan are both 'Beta' and giskard v2 (which had the mature, widely-used tabular/ML scan and RAGET) is 'no longer actively maintained' — so the actively-developed code here is younger and less battle-tested than Giskard's public reputation suggests.

Most of the concrete jailbreak/PII/bias vulnerability catalog is not native: it is delegated to two external optional dependencies bridged in via adapters — 'garak' (pip install giskard-scan[garak], marked 'Heavy dep, not included by default') and 'deepteam' (same caveat) — so depth of coverage for PII entity types, bias metrics, etc. is really garak's/deepteam's, not giskard's own code.

A further scanner, 'lidar', is referenced in integrations/lidar but is explicitly a private Giskard package not published on PyPI (installed from a private git URL) — cannot be evaluated or relied on by an external team.

No standing/runtime request-blocking guardrail middleware ships in this repo; every check/generator is designed to be invoked programmatically (scenario.run()/vulnerability_scan()) as an offline evaluation or CI/red-team step, not as an inline production filter.

Adversarial content generation, jailbreak scenario generation (Crescendo/GOAT/Adversarial rules), and most LLM-as-judge checks (Groundedness, Toxicity, Conformity, Contradiction, AnswerRelevance) require a paid/hosted LLM provider (OpenAI/Anthropic/Google/Azure/LiteLLM) and API key — nothing runs fully offline except the static-dataset/dictionary-style checks (comparison, string/regex matching, JSON schema, rego policy, GCG suffixes, prompt_injection.jsonl).

No stated accuracy/precision-recall benchmark numbers were found for any judge or detector in the source or docs read; reliability rests on the LLM judge's own accuracy and provider quality, which the repo does not quantify.
GCG adversarial suffixes are stated by the maintainers themselves to be English-tuned and 'may not generalize to translated prompts.'
The CHANGELOG explicitly frames this release as migration-focused and not a complete commit history, making it hard to independently verify long-term stability from the changelog alone.
prerequisites: Python 3.12+ (3.13/3.14 also declared supported)
pip install giskard (core+checks) or giskard[scan] for the scanner
An LLM provider SDK + API key (openai/anthropic/google/azure extras, or litellm) for any LLM-as-judge check or LLM-driven scenario generator — required for most of the interesting checks
Optional extras for specific checks: textstat (readability), regorus/celine-regorus (Rego policy), jsonschema (already core), regex (already core)
Optional heavy extras for third-party red-team coverage: giskard-scan[garak] (NVIDIA garak) and giskard-scan[deepteam] (DeepTeam) — both explicitly flagged as heavy and not default-installed
huggingface_hub network access for HuggingFace-dataset-backed generators (do-not-answer-scenarios, harmbench-scenarios)
A private git install of 'lidar' if that optional adapter is to be used (not on PyPI)

reports.integration_effort_reason: Core plumbing is straightforward Python: wrap any Flask/FastAPI endpoint as an async or sync callable target, construct Scenario/Suite objects, and call .run() — the object model (Trace/Interact/Check/CheckResult) is clean and documented with real examples. However, real value (LLM-as-judge checks, adversarial generators, garak/deepteam bridges) requires: (1) provisioning and paying for an LLM provider, (2) installing heavy optional dependencies for garak/deepteam that the maintainers themselves call out as non-trivial, (3) understanding a fairly deep custom abstraction layer (JSONPath-style trace extraction, Jinja2 prompt templates, generic-typed Check classes) before writing custom checks/generators, and (4) accepting that this is pre-1.0 beta software whose API may still shift. No GPU is required for giskard's own code (embeddings/judging are delegated to hosted APIs), but a production Flask/FastAPI integration would need a background job runner since scans are async and can involve many LLM calls per run.
reports.reliability_notes: No quantitative benchmark numbers (precision/recall, attack success rate, detection accuracy) are stated anywhere in the README, CHANGELOG, or source docstrings read. The project is transparent about its own maturity: pyproject.toml classifies it as 'Development Status :: 4 - Beta', the README flags giskard-checks and giskard-scan as '(beta)', and states Giskard v2 (the older, more mature, widely-adopted product) is 'no longer actively maintained.' The test suite is broad in file count (dozens of unit tests per package covering builtin checks, judges, generators, and each integration — garak, deepteam, lidar — plus e2e test files), suggesting reasonable engineering discipline, but breadth of tests does not substitute for stated real-world accuracy metrics. Reliability of the actual vulnerability detection is inherited largely from upstream projects (garak, DeepTeam) and from whichever LLM is configured as the judge, both of which are outside this repo's control and unverified in the files read.
reports.one_line_summary: A modular Python framework (giskard-checks + giskard-scan) for building LLM-as-judge/deterministic evals of agentic systems and for auto-generating red-team/jailbreak/prompt-injection test suites against them, natively and via garak/DeepTeam bridges.

NVIDIA's open-source Colang-driven runtime framework (`nemoguardrails` package) that lets developers wire together dozens of pre-built input/output/retrieval guardrails - LLM self-checks, local ML models, YARA rules, Presidio PII detection, and 15+ third-party moderation APIs - around any LLM application.
reports.core_functionality: The repo is the source for the `nemoguardrails` PyPI package (v0.24.0.dev0, confirmed in pyproject.toml). Its core (nemoguardrails/rails/llm/llmrails.py -> class LLMRails(BaseGuardrails)) wraps an LLM and executes a pipeline of 'rails' (input, output, retrieval, dialog) defined in a Colang DSL (nemoguardrails/colang, .co flow files) and a config.yml/prompts.yml. Each guardrail lives in nemoguardrails/library/<name>/ as a self-contained module with actions.py (the check logic, decorated with @action()), flows.co / flows.v1.co (Colang wiring), rail.py (manifest metadata) and rail_config.py (pydantic config schema). I read actions.py for injection_detection (YARA-based via yara-python), jailbreak_detection (heuristics + model_based + NIM/server modes), self_check/utils.py (generic LLM-judge scaffolding shared by self_check_input/output/facts), sensitive_data_detection/actions.py (Microsoft Presidio + spaCy en_core_web_lg), regex/actions.py (compiled regex matching), content_safety/actions.py (LLM-as-judge call to a configured 'content_safety' model such as Llama Guard/ShieldGemma/Nemotron, plus fast-langdetect based multilingual refusal), hallucination/actions.py (SelfCheckGPT-style self-consistency check via multiple sampled completions + LLM agreement judge), topic_safety/actions.py (LLM-based on-topic/off-topic classifier), context_bloat_detection/actions.py (pure library-based heuristics: size cap, Shannon entropy, longest-run ratio, n-gram repetition ratio to catch context-stuffing/prompt-bloat attacks), factchecking/align_score/actions.py (AlignScore model-based groundedness scoring with fallback to LLM self-check), and gliner/actions.py (NVIDIA GLiNER-PII NIM-based zero-shot NER for PII). I also confirmed ~20 third-party vendor wrapper modules (each with actions.py/rail.py/rail_config.py calling an external hosted API) and a 383-file pytest suite under tests/ (e.g. test_pii_detection_actions.py, test_jailbreak_heuristics.py, test_topic_safety_actions.py) exercising these actions with a RecordingHTTPClient test harness.
key_features: Colang DSL + LLMRails/IORails engines to compose input, output, retrieval, and dialog rails around any LLM (OpenAI, NIM, HF, LangChain-compatible)
Programmable, config-driven rail pipeline (config.yml + prompts.yml) with a plugin-style nemoguardrails/library/ of ~35 built-in and third-party guardrail modules

Built-in jailbreak detection via two statistical heuristics (length/perplexity, prefix-suffix perplexity using GPT2-large) plus a trained random-forest classifier on Snowflake-arctic-embed embeddings, with published benchmark numbers
YARA-rule based injection detection (SQLi, template/Jinja injection, Python code injection, XSS) with reject/omit actions

Presidio (Microsoft) + spaCy based sensitive-data detection/masking supporting all Presidio entity types (PERSON, EMAIL_ADDRESS, CREDIT_CARD, US_SSN, IBAN, phone numbers, etc.) plus custom PatternRecognizers

LLM-as-judge self-check family: self_check_input, self_check_output, self_check_facts/hallucination, content_safety_check_input/output, topic_safety_check_input, using pluggable models (Llama Guard 3, ShieldGemma, Nemotron Content Safety, gpt-oss-safeguard reasoning guards)
AlignScore-based fact-checking/groundedness scorer with automatic fallback to LLM self-check
Context-bloat/context-manipulation detector (entropy, repetition, longest-run, size-cap heuristics) for RAG/agentic prompt-stuffing attacks
IORails tool-calling validation rails that check emitted tool calls and returned tool results against declared JSON schemas (fail-closed, local, no extra LLM calls)
Native integrations with ~20 third-party managed safety/security services (see granular_aspects) for defense-in-depth

granular_aspects.description: YARA rule (sqli.yara) matched against LLM output/tool text; part of injection_detection module.
YARA rule (template.yara) targeting Jinja/template-engine exploitation patterns.
YARA rule (code.yara) for detecting embedded executable code sent to a downstream interpreter.
YARA rule (xss.yara) for markdown/JS injection patterns in LLM output.
Computes input length divided by GPT2-large perplexity; flags jailbreak if score exceeds 89.79 (tuned on AdvBench/ToxicChat/JailbreakChat vs Dolly-15k; 31.19% detection at 7.44% FPR per docs).
Computes GPT2-large perplexity of first/last ~19 words to catch GCG-style adversarial-suffix attacks; default threshold 1845.65 detects 49/50 GCG attacks at 0.04% FPR per docs.
Random-forest classifier trained on Snowflake/snowflake-arctic-embed-m-long embeddings (nemoguardrails/library/jailbreak_detection/model_based/), or delegated to a hosted NIM classification endpoint.

Detects/masks any Microsoft Presidio-supported entity (PERSON, EMAIL_ADDRESS, PHONE_NUMBER, CREDIT_CARD, US_SSN, IBAN_CODE, LOCATION, DATE_TIME, IP_ADDRESS, crypto wallet, etc.) via spaCy en_core_web_lg NLP engine plus custom PatternRecognizers.
Calls an NVIDIA GLiNER-PII NIM/model to detect and mask arbitrary configurable entity types (email, phone_number, ssn, first_name, last_name, credit_debit_card, etc.) without a fixed taxonomy.

LLM-as-judge prompt sent to a configurable content-safety model (Llama Guard 3, ShieldGemma, Nemotron Content Safety NIM, gpt-oss-safeguard) with an is_content_safe output parser; returns safe/unsafe plus violated policy categories (violence, criminal activity, hate speech, sexual content, harassment, self-harm).
fast-langdetect language identification (9 languages: en/es/zh/de/fr/hi/ja/ar/th) to return localized refusal messages when content safety blocks a request.
LLM-as-judge classifies user input as on-topic/off-topic against a configured topic policy prompt, at low temperature (0.01).
Generic LLM self-check scaffolding (self_check/utils.py) reused by self_check_input and self_check_output tasks to ask the main or a dedicated LLM whether text violates policy.
SelfCheckGPT-style check: generates 2 extra sampled completions at temperature 1.0 and asks an LLM judge whether the original response agrees with them.
Calls an external AlignScore model endpoint to score alignment between the bot response and retrieved evidence chunks, falling back to LLM self-check if the endpoint is unavailable.

Library-based heuristics (Shannon entropy, longest repeated-character run ratio, repeated n-gram ratio, absolute size cap) applied cheapest-first to catch prompt-stuffing/context-overflow attacks on input or retrieved RAG chunks.
Arbitrary user-supplied compiled regex patterns matched against input/output/retrieval text (detect_regex_pattern action) for custom forbidden-string rules.

IORails structural rails validate that model-emitted tool calls name a declared tool and match its JSON Schema, and that returned tool results reference a valid tool_call_id; fail-closed, no LLM call.

Generic wrapper (hf_classifier) around any HF text-classification/token-classification model (local transformers, or remote vLLM/KServe/FMS) for toxicity, NER, or custom labels on input/output/retrieval.

Thin action/rail wrappers for ActiveFence, Cisco AI Defense, AutoAlign, Clavata, Cleanlab (trustworthiness score), CrowdStrike AIDR, F5, Fiddler (safety+faithfulness), GCP Text Moderation, Guardrails AI validators, Llama Guard, Pangea AI Guard (deprecated), Patronus AI (Lynx hallucination model), PolicyAI, Polygraf PII, Private AI PII, Prompt Security, Trend Micro Vision One - each requiring its own API key/endpoint.

limitations: Jailbreak detection explicitly 'fails open': per the docs, if the heuristics server or NIM endpoint is unreachable/times out/errors, the request is allowed through with no visible error, silently disabling the protection during an outage.

In-process jailbreak/perplexity checks load a full gpt2-large model via transformers+torch and are explicitly documented as 'NOT RECOMMENDED FOR PRODUCTION' - production use requires standing up a separate heuristics server or GPU NIM.

Detection rates for the built-in heuristics are modest by the maintainers' own published numbers: length/perplexity catches only ~31% of jailbreaks (at 7.4% false-positive rate); heuristics are English-only and produce many false positives on code/non-English text.
Sensitive-data detection (Presidio) requires a large spaCy model (en_core_web_lg) to be separately downloaded and only ships English NLP by default.
Injection-detection 'sanitize' action is explicitly unimplemented (_sanitize_injection raises NotImplementedError); only reject/omit are usable.

A large fraction of the 'catalog' (ActiveFence, Cisco AI Defense, AutoAlign, Clavata, CrowdStrike AIDR, F5, Fiddler, Pangea, Patronus AI, PolicyAI, Polygraf, Private AI, Prompt Security, Trend Micro, GCP) are thin wrappers requiring a paid/hosted third-party API key - the OSS repo itself does not perform the detection, it just calls out.

Content-safety, topic-safety, and self-check rails are only as good as the underlying LLM/judge model configured - no fixed accuracy number is provided in-repo for these since they depend on whichever model the integrator plugs in.
Tool-calling/IORails validation and OpenTelemetry tracing are marked experimental/opt-in and not available on the default LLMRails engine.

Base install: aiohttp, pydantic, jinja2, lark (Colang parser), fastembed/onnxruntime, simpleeval, typer
Optional 'sdd' extra: presidio-analyzer/presidio-anonymizer + spaCy en_core_web_lg model download for sensitive-data detection
Optional 'jailbreak' extra: yara-python (for injection_detection) plus transformers+torch (only for local/dev jailbreak perplexity checks - GPT2-large)
Optional 'multilingual' extra: fast-langdetect (downloads a ~125MB fastText model on first use)
Optional 'server' extra: fastapi, uvicorn, openai client, starlette
A configured LLM backend (OpenAI-compatible, NVIDIA NIM, or LangChain-compatible model) for every LLM-as-judge rail (content safety, topic safety, self-check, hallucination, fact-checking)
API keys/endpoints for any of the ~15 third-party vendor integrations actually enabled (e.g. ACTIVEFENCE_API_KEY, PAI_API_KEY, AI_DEFENSE_API_KEY, CLEANLAB_API_KEY, etc.)
reports.integration_effort_reason: Core library is pure-Python, pip-installable, and async-native, so calling `LLMRails.generate_async()` from a FastAPI/Flask backend is straightforward (the package even ships its own optional FastAPI server and OpenAI-compatible /v1/checks endpoint). However, real effort scales with which rails are enabled: purely library-based rails (regex, context-bloat, injection YARA) are near drop-in; LLM-as-judge rails (content safety, topic safety, self-check, hallucination) require configuring and hosting a capable judge model and writing/adapting prompts.yml; Presidio/GLiNER PII rails require extra model downloads (spaCy en_core_web_lg, GLiNER NIM); and any of the ~15 third-party vendor rails require signing up for and wiring in a separate paid API. Colang flow authoring (.co files) is a non-trivial DSL a team must learn to customize dialog-level rails beyond the pre-built catalog.
reports.reliability_notes: This is the official NVIDIA-maintained OSS package (NVIDIA-NeMo/Guardrails, PyPI `nemoguardrails`, backed by an arXiv paper arXiv:2310.10501) with CI badges for Linux/Windows/macOS tests and lint, a 383-file pytest suite exercising nearly every library action (test_jailbreak_heuristics.py, test_pii_detection_actions.py, test_topic_safety_actions.py, etc.) using a RecordingHTTPClient harness, and an actively maintained CHANGELOG (version 0.24.0.dev0 in-repo, latest release 0.23.0 dated 2026-07-01) with dozens of tracked GitHub issues/PRs (issue numbers past #2100). The maintainers are unusually transparent about weak points: they publish exact false-positive/detection-rate numbers for the jailbreak heuristics and explicitly flag that jailbreak detection 'fails open' on detector outage and that in-process perplexity checks are not production-ready. Reliability of the LLM-as-judge rails (content safety, topic safety, hallucination, self-check) is inherently dependent on whatever external LLM/judge model an integrator supplies and is not benchmarked in-repo.
reports.afni_fit_note: Best positioned as the runtime orchestration/enforcement layer of a unified AFNI toolkit - its Colang/config-driven input-output-retrieval rail pipeline can host AFNI's own detectors (regex, PII, jailbreak) as first-class rails while also acting as the integration point for other reviewed repos' models (e.g. plugging a groundedness or bias scorer in as a custom 'action') and for paid vendor APIs the org already has contracts with.

Best used as the runtime backbone, not the detector library: adopt Guard/AsyncGuard plus the RAIL/Pydantic schema and reask engine as the input/output gateway in front of AFNI's Python backend (or via the bundled Flask server as an OpenAI-compatible proxy), then plug in whichever concrete detectors AFNI needs — either vetted `guardrails-ai-<name>` Hub packages or custom in-house `@register_validator` classes for PII, secrets, toxicity, groundedness, etc. — while separately tracking the Hub-migration timeline and the 0.10.1 supply-chain incident as vendor-risk items.
reports.core_functionality: The `guardrails/` package's `Guard`/`AsyncGuard` classes (guardrails/guard.py, guardrails/async_guard.py) are the main entry points: they compile an output schema (RAIL XML via guardrails/schema/rail_schema.py + lxml, a Pydantic BaseModel via schema/pydantic_schema.py, or a plain string/primitive via schema/primitive_schema.py) into a ProcessedSchema, call an LLM provider (guardrails/llm_providers.py, via litellm/openai/anthropic SDKs), then run a Runner/AsyncRunner/StreamRunner (guardrails/run/*.py) that executes each attached Validator's `_validate()` and applies an OnFailAction (NOOP/EXCEPTION/REASK/FIX/FILTER/REFRAIN/FIX_REASK, guardrails/types/on_fail.py) with automatic reask-prompt construction on failure. Validators themselves are NOT implemented in this repo: guardrails/validators/__init__.py only re-exports the base Validator/ValidationResult classes from guardrails/validator_base.py, and guardrails/hub/__init__.py dynamically resolves validator names (e.g. `guardrails/detect_pii`) by reading a project-local `.guardrails/hub_registry.json` and importlib-importing them from standalone public-PyPI packages named `guardrails-ai-<validator>` (namespace package `guardrails_ai.*`), a migration explicitly called out in the README as replacing the old private Guardrails Hub/remote-inference registry (cutoff Aug 6, 2026 per the file). Supporting subsystems read: guardrails/cli/ (Typer-based `guardrails configure|create|start|validate|watch`), guardrails/classes/history/ (Call/Iteration audit trail), guardrails/telemetry + hub_telemetry/ (OpenTelemetry tracing), guardrails/validator_service/ (parallel/async/multiprocess validator execution), and guardrails/integrations/ (LangChain Runnable, LlamaIndex, Databricks).

granular_aspects.description: guardrails/schema/rail_schema.py and pydantic_schema.py compile RAIL XML or Pydantic models into a JSON-Schema-validated ProcessedSchema (types: string, integer, float, boolean, object, list, email, url); guardrails/schema/validator.py performs full JSON Schema compliance checks and reports which field failed.

Deterministic FIX / FILTER / REFRAIN handling plus automatic REASK (re-prompting the LLM with the exact validator error) implemented in guardrails/run/runner.py and guardrails/merge.py, giving an auditable, policy-driven remediation path rather than a silent pass/fail.

guardrails/classes/history/call.py and iteration.py record every raw LLM output, parsed/validated output, validator-level pass/fail result, token counts and timing for each Guard invocation, retrievable via guard.history for audit trails.

Validator.validate_stream() (guardrails/validator_base.py) attaches character-offset ErrorSpan objects to FailResults on streamed chunks, so a UI can highlight exactly which substring of a token-streamed LLM response failed validation.

reports.integration_effort_reason: Wiring the core framework into a Python/Flask/FastAPI backend is genuinely low effort — `Guard().use(SomeValidator(...))` plus either direct `guard.validate()` calls or standing up the bundled Flask `guardrails start` server with an OpenAI-SDK-compatible proxy endpoint requires little glue code. Effort rises to Medium/High once you need actual detectors: each concrete check is a separate PyPI package to vet and install, some require torch/transformers or GPU-backed local inference now that hosted remote inference is being sunset, the Hub ecosystem is actively migrating (deprecated CLI paths, changing import locations from `guardrails.hub` to `guardrails_ai.*`), and the May-2026 supply-chain incident means any adoption should pin exact versions and review signed commits before installing hub packages.

Parallelized validator execution via asyncio plus a separate-process executor for CPU/ML-heavy synchronous validators
Guardrails Server: a Flask app (`guardrails start`) exposing REST + an OpenAI-SDK-compatible endpoint so guards can front an existing OpenAI integration with no client code changes

CLI (`guardrails configure/create/start/validate/watch`) built on Typer, with deprecated `hub install/uninstall/submit/create-validator` subcommands now shimmed to plain `pip install guardrails-ai-<name>`

limitations: The core repository at this path ships NO concrete detectors itself: guardrails/validators/__init__.py only re-exports the Validator/ValidationResult base classes, and every named check (PII, toxicity, secrets, provenance/groundedness, SQL/Python syntax, topic restriction, competitor check, etc.) is dynamically imported from separately versioned, separately maintained `guardrails-ai-<name>` PyPI packages via guardrails/hub/. Anyone evaluating 'what checks does Guardrails ship' must audit those external packages, not this repo.

The project is mid-migration away from its old hosted Guardrails Hub / remote-inference service: README.md states validators are moving to standard PyPI with a stated cutoff date, and guardrails-features-list.md marks `hub install/uninstall/create-validator/submit` CLI subcommands as Deprecated shims — meaning some documented workflows in docs/examples/*.ipynb (which still show `guardrails hub install ...` style usage in places) may not reflect the current install path.

SECURITY_ADVISORY.md (in-repo) documents a real supply-chain compromise: a malicious `guardrails-ai==0.10.1` was published to PyPI after a maintainer's GitHub PAT was stolen as part of a broader multi-repo campaign; users were told to pin to 0.10.0 or install from a signed git tag. This is a direct trust/reliability caveat for a governance-tooling vendor and should factor into any AFNI vendor-risk assessment.

ML-based checks (e.g. ToxicLanguage's HuggingFace model) previously leaned on a hosted 'remote inference' service that is being discontinued; teams must now self-host the underlying models (torch/transformers, optional GPU) or find another inference path, adding real infra work beyond `pip install`.

No jailbreak-detection, prompt-injection, or adversarial red-teaming logic was found anywhere in this repo's source (guardrails/, tests/); this is purely an enforcement/orchestration framework, not an attack or fuzz-testing tool.

Windows/PowerShell environment here could not execute `make test`/pytest to confirm the 93 test_*.py files actually pass against the current dependency set noted in CLAUDE.md as a required gate; test presence was verified by file listing/reading only, not by running the suite.
reports.one_line_summary: A Python orchestration framework (Guard/AsyncGuard classes, RAIL/Pydantic schemas, reask loop, CLI, Flask/FastAPI server) that wires composable input/output 'validators' around LLM calls; the concrete detectors themselves (PII, toxicity, secrets, jailbreak-adjacent checks, etc.) now live in separately-versioned Guardrails Hub packages rather than in this codebase.

pip/poetry install of `guardrails-ai`; `guardrails configure` to create a local `.guardrailsrc`
An LLM API credential (OpenAI/Anthropic/Azure/Gemini/Databricks key, or a LiteLLM-supported provider, or local Ollama) for any Guard that actually calls an LLM
Separate `pip install guardrails-ai-<validator>` per desired Hub check (e.g. guardrails-ai-detect-pii, guardrails-ai-toxic-language) — these are not bundled

reports.reliability_notes: README claims an external benchmark ('Guardrails Index', index.guardrailsai.com) comparing 24 guardrails across 6 categories, but no benchmark numbers or methodology are present in this repo to verify. In-repo evidence of engineering maturity: CI workflows (.github/workflows/ci.yml, premerge.yml, server_ci.yml, dependency-audit.yml, cli-compatibility.yml), pyright type-checking, ruff linting, a 93-file test_*.py suite split into unit_tests/ and integration_tests/, and a documented dependency-security process in CLAUDE.md (wide pyproject ranges for compatibility, pinned poetry.lock for security, three required gates: lint/type/test). Against that, SECURITY_ADVISORY.md records an actual critical supply-chain compromise (malicious guardrails-ai 0.10.1 on PyPI, stolen GitHub PAT, org-wide token rotation) — a concrete negative reliability signal for a project positioned as governance infrastructure. Because all concrete detectors now live outside this repo, no accuracy/precision/recall data for any specific check (PII, toxicity, groundedness, etc.) is observable from this codebase.

reports.one_line_summary: A TypeScript/Bun library (@presidio-dev/hai-guardrails, npm) that wraps a set of composable 'guards' (injection, leakage, PII, secrets, toxicity, hate speech, bias, adult content, copyright, profanity) around LLM chat messages, each guard pluggable with a heuristic, regex-pattern, or LLM-judge detection tactic.
reports.core_functionality: The repo is organized around a small core (src/engine, src/guards, src/tactics, src/types, src/bridge). `GuardrailsEngine` (src/engine/index.ts) takes an array of 'guards' and runs each sequentially over an array of chat messages, hashing each message (SHA256/512 via src/utils/hash.ts), tracking which messages are 'in scope' per guard (role/selection filters implemented in src/guards/make.ts's selectMessages, covering All/First/Last/NFirst/NLast selection types with role filtering), applying any redaction the guard produces, and returning both the (possibly modified) messages and a structured per-guard result set. Each concrete guard (injection.guard.ts, leakage.guard.ts, pii.guard.ts, secret.guard.ts, and the LLM-based ones built on llm.guard.ts) is built via a `makeGuard` factory (src/guards/make.ts) that wraps a guard-specific `implementation` function returning a GuardResult (passed/reason/score/modifiedMessage). Three 'tactics' are implemented in src/tactics/: Heuristic (fuzzy/word-overlap matching against a keyword list, executed in a Piscina worker-thread pool — src/workers/heuristic.worker.ts — for parallelism), Pattern (plain regex matching, src/tactics/pattern.tactic.ts), and LanguageModel (renders a scoring prompt and calls a LangChain `BaseChatModel` or a user-supplied LLM callback, parses a float 0-1 score, src/tactics/language-model.tactic.ts). The generic `llmGuard` (src/guards/llm.guard.ts) is the workhorse behind all the content-moderation guards: it builds a system prompt embedding a Zod JSON schema plus few-shot valid/invalid examples, calls the LLM, repairs/parses the JSON response with `jsonrepair`, validates it against the Zod schema, and returns pass/fail (Binary) or score-vs-threshold (Score). PII and Secret guards are pure deterministic regex+entropy scanners with no LLM dependency (redactPII/redactSecrets functions), computing Shannon entropy to reduce false positives on secret patterns. A LangChain bridge (src/bridge/langchain.bridge.ts, src/bridge/transformer/langchain/*) lets the engine wrap a LangChain chat model transparently. Examples in examples/*.ts (pii.ts, secret.ts, injection.ts, toxic.ts, bias-detection.ts, etc.) and examples/apps/langchain-chat show real usage; a Bun test file (src/guards/make.test.ts) unit-tests the selectMessages scope logic exhaustively (13 cases) but is the only test file found in the repo — no tests for the regex/entropy detectors or the LLM-scoring guards themselves.
key_features: Composable GuardrailsEngine that chains multiple guards over an LLM message array and returns per-guard structured results plus redacted/modified messages
Three pluggable detection tactics per applicable guard: heuristic fuzzy-keyword matching (worker-thread pool via Piscina), static regex pattern matching, and LLM-as-judge scoring
Generic llmGuard factory: define any custom LLM-based check via a Zod schema, role-definition prompt, and few-shot valid/invalid examples — used to build all 6 content-moderation guards

Deterministic PII guard with 10 default regex entities (email, phone, SSN, credit card, IP, ICD-10, MRN numeric, MRN alphanumeric, NPI, DEA) supporting redact or block mode, and user-extensible pattern list

Deterministic Secret guard with ~24 default credential/token regex signatures (1Password, AWS access/secret key, Azure AD client secret, GitHub PAT/fine-grained-PAT/OAuth/App/refresh tokens, ~14 distinct GitLab token types) each with a minimum Shannon-entropy gate to cut false positives
Message hashing (SHA-256/SHA-512 selectable) to track messages across guard passes and correlate modified content back to original messages
Message selection/scoping helper (selectMessages) supporting role filters and All/First/Last/NFirst/NLast selection strategies
LangChain bridge (LangChainChatGuardrails) to wrap any LangChain BaseChatModel transparently with the guardrails engine
Bring-your-own-provider (BYOP) support: guards accept any custom LLM function, not just LangChain models
Structured logging via Pino with configurable log levels

granular_aspects.description: injection.guard.ts generates a large combinatorial keyword list (verbs like Ignore/Disregard/Bypass x adjectives x objects x prepositions) and scores input via fuzzy string-similarity/word-overlap (Heuristic tactic, string-similarity lib).

~18 static regexes for common injection phrasings ('ignore previous instructions', 'you are now', 'act as', 'jailbreak', 'developer mode', 'as an AI', role-prefix spoofing like 'system:'/'assistant:', etc.).
LanguageModel tactic sends a hand-written few-shot prompt asking the LLM to output a single 0.0-1.0 injection-likelihood float.

leakage.guard.ts mirrors the injection guard's 3-tactic design with its own keyword list (~21 phrases) and regex set (~9 patterns) targeting attempts to extract system prompt/hidden instructions/config, plus an LLM-judge prompt variant.
Regex entity in PII_REGEX_REGISTRY, redacts to [REDACTED-EMAIL].
Regex for XXX-XXX-XXXX style numbers.
Regex for XXX-XX-XXXX pattern (also collides with generic 9-digit formats).
Regex for 16-digit grouped numbers.
Regex for dotted-quad IPv4 addresses.
Regex-based healthcare PHI entity added in v1.11.0 for ICD-10 codes.
Two regex variants (numeric 7-10 digit, and alphanumeric with MR/MRN prefix) for healthcare PHI.
Regex for 10-digit NPI numbers with NPI prefix.
Regex for DEA-registration-style alphanumeric codes.

secret.guard.ts ships ~24 provider-specific regex signatures (1Password token/secret key, AWS access/secret token, Azure AD client secret, GitHub PAT/fine-grained PAT/OAuth/App/refresh tokens, and ~14 distinct GitLab token types: CI/CD job, deploy, feature-flag, feed, incoming-mail, k8s agent, OAuth app secret, PAT, routable PAT, pipeline trigger, runner registration, runner auth token + routable, SCIM token, session cookie), each gated by a computed Shannon-entropy minimum to reduce false positives; redact or block mode.
toxic.guard.ts is an LLM-judge (via llmGuard/ValidationType.Score) rating general toxic/harassing/demeaning language 0-1, default threshold 0.95, with few-shot examples.

hate-speech.guard.ts is an LLM-judge specifically for identity-based attacks (race, ethnicity, religion, gender identity, sexual orientation, disability); returns categories and targetedGroups fields.
bias-detection.guard.ts is an LLM-judge detecting stereotypes/unfair generalizations by group membership, returning categories (age/gender/racial etc.), affectedGroups, and impact (low/medium/high).
adult-content.guard.ts LLM-judge flags explicit sexual content/adult themes, returns categories and isExplicit boolean.
copyright.guard.ts LLM-judge flags likely copyrighted text (lyrics, book excerpts, code, scripts), returns type, source, isDirectMatch fields.
profanity.guard.ts LLM-judge flags swear words/vulgar language, returns flaggedWords list and severity (mild/moderate/severe).

llm.guard.ts's llmGuard() lets a team define arbitrary Zod-schema-validated LLM checks (Binary pass/fail or Score-vs-threshold) with reason fields for explainability, used as the base for all 6 content-safety guards above.
selectMessages (src/guards/make.ts) deterministically marks which messages in a conversation a guard should evaluate (role filter x All/First/Last/NFirst/NLast), unit-tested in make.test.ts.

limitations: Almost no automated test coverage for the actual detectors: the only test file (src/guards/make.test.ts) tests message-selection scoping logic, not the regex/entropy PII-secret matchers or the LLM-scoring guards' accuracy — there are no documented precision/recall/benchmark numbers anywhere in the repo.

The 6 content-moderation guards (toxic, hate-speech, bias-detection, adult-content, copyright, profanity) and the LLM tactic for injection/leakage are entirely LLM-judge based with hard-coded few-shot examples baked into the source; behavior is only as good as whatever LLM the integrating team supplies, and results depend on that LLM reliably returning parseable JSON/floats (mitigated by jsonrepair but not guaranteed).

PII/secret regexes are simple and generic (e.g., SSN and phone/credit-card regexes are loose digit-grouping patterns prone to false positives/negatives; no Luhn checksum validation for credit cards, no NER/context model), so accuracy is inherently limited compared to ML-based PII detectors like Presidio.

Maturity/activity signal is limited to what's visible locally: CHANGELOG shows steady but modest feature-release cadence (v1.6-v1.11 over ~3 months in 2025) from a small maintainer set (presidio-oss, an unrelated company also named Presidio, not the Microsoft Presidio project) — no GitHub star/fork counts, issue counts, or CI test-pass badges could be verified from the local checkout.
TypeScript/Node/Bun only — no Python bindings or REST/HTTP server included, so a Python/Flask/FastAPI backend cannot call it in-process and would need a Node microservice/sidecar plus network glue.

Guard prompts, keyword lists, and regex patterns are hard-coded in source (not centrally configurable via files), so customization requires forking or passing override arrays through the (large) opts objects.
prerequisites: Node.js >=16 or Bun >=1.0 runtime (TypeScript-first, ESM/CJS dual build)
@langchain/core ^1.1.19 peer dependency for LangChain-based LLM tactics/bridge (a LangChain BaseChatModel instance) OR a custom BYOP LLM function

An LLM/API key (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc., via LangChain, or self-hosted model) required for all 6 content-moderation guards and the language-model tactic of injection/leakage guards — the PII and Secret guards work standalone with zero LLM/API dependency
npm dependencies: zod (schema validation), jsonrepair (LLM JSON output repair), piscina (worker-thread pool for heuristic tactic), string-similarity, pino (logging), ts-pattern
reports.integration_effort_reason: The library itself is a small, well-factored TypeScript SDK with a clean functional API (import a guard function, instantiate GuardrailsEngine, call .run()) — trivial to wire up inside a Node/TypeScript service. However, since the target stack is Python/Flask/FastAPI, a team would need to either (a) run this as a separate Node/Bun microservice and call it over HTTP/gRPC (no server is shipped, so that wrapper must be written), or (b) reimplement the regex/entropy PII and secret patterns natively in Python (straightforward, they're just regex tables) while dropping the LLM-judge guards or reimplementing their prompts directly against the Python backend's own LLM client (moderate effort, prompts and Zod schemas are documented/readable). No GPU needed; an LLM API/model is required only for injection/leakage's language-model mode and all 6 content-moderation guards.
reports.reliability_notes: No independent benchmark numbers, accuracy metrics, or red-team evaluation results are documented in the repo or docs. Reliability signals present: a CHANGELOG showing active, versioned releases (semantic-release with commitlint/conventional-changelog, RC pre-releases, up to v1.11.0), a CI/CD badge referencing build provenance attestation, and one focused unit-test file for message-scoping logic. There is no test coverage demonstrating detector accuracy, and the LLM-judge guards' reliability is entirely dependent on the caller-supplied model faithfully following the few-shot prompt and returning valid JSON (jsonrepair is a safety net, not a guarantee). The deterministic PII/secret regexes are simple pattern-matching without contextual/statistical validation beyond Shannon entropy for secrets, so false-positive/negative rates are unverified and likely non-trivial for generic PII types (SSN/phone/credit-card regexes especially).
reports.afni_fit_note: Best used as the deterministic tier (PII regex + entropy-gated secret scanning + regex/heuristic injection-leakage screens) ported or proxied into AFNI's Python stack for zero-LLM-cost pre-filtering, while its 6 content-moderation guards serve as a reference prompt/schema library for building AFNI's own LLM-judge layer (toxicity, hate speech, bias, adult content, copyright, profanity) rather than being called live cross-language from Flask/FastAPI.

The moderationlayer→moderationmodel pair already implements almost exactly the unified guardrail-orchestrator pattern AFNI needs: one async dispatcher (callModerationModels/validation_input in service.py) fans out to ~15 independently-thresholded checks and returns a single pass/fail summary with per-check evidence — this could be lifted wholesale as the orchestration layer, with the privacy (Presidio-based), fairness (aif360/fairlearn), and hallucination (RAG+G-Eval) modules plugged in as backing scanners, and the vendored TrustLLM package reused for periodic offline benchmarking.
reports.core_functionality: This is a ~20-microservice Python (FastAPI) + Angular monorepo. Its center of gravity is responsible-ai-moderationlayer/src/service/service.py (170KB), whose validation_input class and callModerationModels() dispatcher asynchronously POST the same input text to a sibling service, responsible-ai-moderationmodel (src/service/*.py), which hosts locally-loaded fine-tuned HuggingFace transformers (toxicity, prompt-injection, restricted-topic, ban-code, gibberish) plus a shared SentenceTransformer (multi-qa-mpnet-base-dot-v1) whose embeddings are cosine-compared against pre-computed JSON embedding banks (jailbreak_embeddings.json ~1.7MB, refusal_embeddings.json, topic_embeddings.json, orgpolicy_embeddings.json) to flag jailbreaks, refusals, restricted topics and org-policy violations. Separate sibling services cover privacy (a customized Presidio analyzer plus Faker-based anonymization across text/PDF/DOCX/PPTX/XLSX/CSV/JSON/images/DICOM/video), safety/toxicity (Detoxify + better_profanity + NudeNet/nsfw-detector for image/video nudity + a codebert-based malicious-URL classifier), fairness (aif360 + fairlearn wrapped in a bespoke infosys_responsible_ai_fairness pip package, plus vision-LLM-based image-bias review), Hallucination/RAG (LangChain-driven retrieval-similarity scoring blended with a G-Eval LLM-judge over faithfulness/relevance/adherence/correctness), and explainability (SHAP/LIME for tabular models, prompt-based Token Importance, and CoT/CoVe/ThoT/GoT reasoning templates for LLM answers). A vendored trustllm_pkg implements the academic TrustLLM benchmark (ethics/fairness/privacy/robustness/safety/truthfulness tasks) as an offline evaluation harness. All checks are driven by per-account/portfolio thresholds configured through a separate admin service and consumed by an Angular micro-frontend (mfe/shell).
key_features: Single async orchestrator (moderationlayer) that fans a prompt/response out to ~15 independently-thresholded checks and returns one PASSED/FAILED summary with per-check evidence, in both coupled (with LLM call) and decoupled modes

Locally-hosted fine-tuned transformer models for toxicity, prompt-injection, restricted-topic (zero-shot DeBERTa + fine-tuned DistilBERT), ban-code and gibberish detection, no external API required for these checks
Embedding-similarity engine (SentenceTransformer multi-qa-mpnet-base-dot-v1) reused across jailbreak, refusal, restricted-topic and org-policy checks against large pre-computed embedding banks

Presidio-derived privacy engine supporting 30 PII entity types across text and 9+ file/media formats (PDF, Office docs, images via Azure OCR, DICOM medical images, video) with Faker-based anonymization, encryption and differential-privacy options

Fairness engine combining AIF360 and Fairlearn metrics/mitigations with a custom pip package (infosys_responsible_ai_fairness) plus multimodal (GPT-4o/Gemini/Mixtral/Llama/AWS) LLM review of generated images for demographic bias

RAG hallucination scorer blending embedding-similarity (input-output, response-source, input-source) with a 4-criterion G-Eval LLM-judge, plus CoT/Chain-of-Verification/Thread-of-Thought/Graph-of-Thought reasoning add-ons
Vendored TrustLLM benchmark package for offline LLM evaluation across ethics, fairness, privacy, robustness, safety and truthfulness tasks
SHAP/LIME classic-ML explainability, prompt-based Token Importance for LLM outputs, and vision-LLM (GPT-4o/Gemini/Ollama) prompt-based explanation of generated images

Admin service for per-account/portfolio configuration of custom PII recognizers, restricted-topic lists, custom themes and per-check thresholds, backed by Mongo-style DAOs and an Elasticsearch telemetry pipeline
Multi-provider LLM abstraction (Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Llama3, Bloom) baked into the moderation layer's completion classes

granular_aspects.description: Fine-tuned DistilBERT classifier (models/fine_tuned_promptInjection_model) run behind an /injection endpoint, with an optional switch to an Azure/AICloud-hosted prompt-injection model; returns a confidence score compared to a configurable threshold.

SentenceTransformer (multi-qa-mpnet-base-dot-v1) embeds the input and cosine-compares it against jailbreak_embeddings.json, a ~1.7MB pre-computed bank of known jailbreak-prompt embeddings; highest similarity above threshold triggers FAILED.

Two interchangeable backends: a zero-shot DeBERTa (restricted-deberta-base-zeroshot-v2) multi-label classifier against admin-configured topic labels, and a fine-tuned DistilBERT multi-label model; seeded example topics in topics.json cover terrorism/violence, cyberattacks, exam/academic dishonesty, corporate/professional ethics violations and other illegal activity.
Cosine similarity of the model response against refusal_embeddings.json, a bank of canned LLM-refusal phrase embeddings, to detect unwanted or unwanted-absent refusals.
Embedding similarity against orgpolicy_embeddings.json / theme-specific embeddings so a tenant can block content resembling an internally-defined restricted theme or company policy statement.
Fine-tuned sequence classifier (models/bancode) that flags source-code content after markdown/list/number stripping preprocessing, to prevent code smuggling in prompts/responses.
